```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 2.4,
  dpi = 110,
  fig.align = "center"
)
```

```{r libs, message = FALSE}
library(brouillet)
library(ggplot2)
```

Every exported function appears below, with a runnable example. Two helpers are
used throughout to show results: `swatch()` draws a set of discrete colours,
`band()` draws a gradient across a range.

```{r helpers}
swatch <- function(colors, title = NULL) {
  df <- data.frame(i = seq_along(colors), fill = colors)
  discrete <- length(colors) <= 24
  ggplot(df, aes(i, 1, fill = fill)) +
    geom_tile(colour = if (discrete) "white" else NA,
              linewidth = if (discrete) 1.5 else 0) +
    scale_fill_identity() +
    labs(title = title, x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme_void(base_size = 9) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 9, hjust = 0))
}

band <- function(params, limits = c(0, 1), title = NULL, from = limits[1],
                 to = limits[2]) {
  x <- seq(from, to, length.out = 400)
  df <- data.frame(x = x, fill = asColorFun(params, limits = limits)(x))
  ggplot(df, aes(x, 1, fill = fill)) +
    geom_raster() +
    scale_fill_identity() +
    scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
    labs(title = title, x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
    theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank(),
          plot.title = element_text(size = 9))
}
```

# Specifications

A specification describes a gradient without reference to any data, so the same
object works on any range.

## `gradientParams()`

The main constructor.

```{r gradientParams}
p <- gradientParams(
  colors    = c("navy", "white", "firebrick"),
  midpoints = 0.5,
  center    = 0.5,
  width     = 0.3
)
p
```

```{r gradientParams-band}
band(p, c(-2, 2), "gradientParams(width = 0.3) over -2 to 2")
```

`midpoints` places the colour stops as fractions of the range;
`center`/`width`/`asymmetry` shape the curve inside each segment. `space`,
`interpolate`, `rescale`, the clip colours and `gradient_mode` are covered in
their own sections below.

## `gradientTemplate()`

The same arguments without `colors`: a shape waiting for a palette. Useful when
the curve is a house style but the colours change per figure.

```{r gradientTemplate}
house <- gradientTemplate(width = 0.25, high.clip.color = "gold")
house
```

A template cannot be plotted until it has colours; every converter refuses it
with a message saying so.

## `withColors()`

Completes a template, or swaps the palette of a finished specification.

```{r withColors}
withColors(house, c("black", "orange"))

withColors(p, c("grey90", "darkgreen"))$colors
```

```{r withColors-band}
band(withColors(house, c("black", "orange")), title = "the house curve, new palette")
```

## `updateGradient()`

Changes fields and revalidates. `NULL` resets a field to its default.

```{r updateGradient}
updateGradient(p, width = 0.1)$width

updateGradient(p, high.clip.color = "gold")$high.clip.color

updateGradient(p, high.clip.color = NULL)$high.clip.color

tryCatch(updateGradient(p, widht = 0.1), error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
```

Changing the palette length drops stale midpoints rather than failing:

```{r updateGradient-warn}
withCallingHandlers(
  updateGradient(p, colors = c("navy", "firebrick"))$midpoints,
  warning = function(w) {
    message("warned: ", conditionMessage(w))
    invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
  }
)
```

## `reverseGradient()`

Mirrors a specification: colours, midpoints, `center` and `asymmetry` all flip,
and the clip colours swap. Reversing twice is the identity.

```{r reverseGradient}
asym <- gradientParams(c("navy", "white", "firebrick"), midpoints = 0.4,
                       center = 0.3, asymmetry = 0.5)
rev_asym <- reverseGradient(asym)

c(midpoints = rev_asym$midpoints, center = rev_asym$center,
  asymmetry = rev_asym$asymmetry)
```

```{r reverseGradient-band, fig.height = 3.4}
library(patchwork)
band(asym, title = "original") / band(rev_asym, title = "reversed")
```

# Shaping the curve

## `contrastCurve()`

The S-shaped mapping from position-in-data to position-in-ramp. `center` is the
50% point, `width` the span from 5% to 95%, `asymmetry` which side rolls off
slowly.

```{r contrastCurve}
x <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 20001)
y <- contrastCurve(x, center = 0.7, width = 0.2)

x[which(y >= 0.5)[1]]
x[which(y >= 0.95)[1]] - x[which(y >= 0.05)[1]]
```

```{r contrastCurve-plot, fig.height = 3}
curves <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  list(c(0.5, 1.0, 0), c(0.5, 0.4, 0), c(0.5, 0.12, 0),
       c(0.5, 0.4, 0.8), c(0.3, 0.4, 0)),
  function(k) data.frame(x = x, y = contrastCurve(x, k[1], k[2], k[3]),
                         setting = sprintf("center %.2g, width %.2g, asym %.1f",
                                           k[1], k[2], k[3]))
))

ggplot(curves, aes(x, y, colour = setting)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = 3, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "position in data", y = "position in ramp", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

## `doubleSigmoid()`

A four-parameter curve: the product of two logistic factors, and the mapping
brouillet used before 0.2. Because the factors multiply, the curve stays near
zero until the *later* inflexion point, then jumps to whatever level the earlier
factor has reached and continues gradually -- a hard threshold followed by a
slow ramp, ending short of 1. `contrastCurve()` cannot do that: it is continuous
at its centre and is rescaled to reach both ends.

```{r doubleSigmoid}
f <- doubleSigmoid(sigma1 = 200, sigma2 = 200,
                   inflexpoint1 = 0.3, inflexpoint2 = 0.4)
round(f(seq(0, 1, 0.25)), 3)

threshold <- doubleSigmoid(sigma1 = 500, sigma2 = 5,
                           inflexpoint1 = 0.3, inflexpoint2 = 0.6)
round(threshold(seq(0, 1, 0.1)), 2)
```

```{r doubleSigmoid-band}
band(gradientParams(c("navy", "firebrick"), curve_fun = threshold),
     title = "doubleSigmoid(500, 5, 0.3, 0.6): nothing, then a jump, then a ramp")
```

Two sharp factors give a single step at the later inflexion point rather than
two steps, since multiplying two rising curves acts as an AND. Note also that
the result is not rescaled, so the end colours are approached rather than
reached.

## `curve_fun`

Any function from [0, 1] to [0, 1] can replace the built-in curve. It applies
**within each segment**, unlike `mapping_fun`, which applies once across the
whole colour list.

```{r curve-fun}
band(gradientParams(c("navy", "white", "firebrick"), midpoints = 0.5,
                    curve_fun = function(u) u^3),
     title = "curve_fun = u^3, applied in both segments")
```

## `steepnessPresets()`

The named sigma pairs from the pre-0.2 API, kept so old settings can be
reproduced.

```{r steepnessPresets}
steepnessPresets()
```

# Clipping

## Clip colours on a specification

Out-of-range values take their own colours, shown as bands on the colourbar.

```{r clip}
clipped <- gradientParams(c("navy", "white", "firebrick"), midpoints = 0.5,
                          width = 0.3,
                          low.clip.color = "grey35", high.clip.color = "gold")

asColorFun(clipped, limits = c(-2, 2))(c(-99, -2, 0, 2, 99, NA))
```

```{r clip-band}
band(clipped, limits = c(-2, 2), from = -2.6, to = 2.6,
     title = "drawn beyond the limits: clip colours at both ends")
```

`blend.clip = TRUE` fades the clip colour in over the first 10% beyond each
limit instead of switching abruptly:

```{r blend-clip}
band(updateGradient(clipped, blend.clip = TRUE), limits = c(-2, 2),
     from = -2.6, to = 2.6, title = "blend.clip = TRUE")
```

## `clippingGradient()`

Works on a stop table rather than a specification: restricts it to a window and
appends one stop just outside each end.

```{r clippingGradient}
g <- sigmoidGradient2("navy", "firebrick", width = 0.3)
cl <- clippingGradient(g, low.value = 0.2, high.value = 0.8,
                       low.clip.color = "grey80", high.clip.color = "black")

head(cl, 3)
range(cl$value)
```

## `blendingClippingGradient()`

The same, with the clip colours fading into the ends.

```{r blendingClippingGradient}
bl <- blendingClippingGradient(g, 0, 1, "grey80", "black")
nrow(bl)
head(bl$color, 4)
```

# Using a specification

## `asColorFun()`

A vectorised value-to-colour function, interface-compatible with
`circlize::colorRamp2()`, so it drives ComplexHeatmap, base graphics and raster
export as well as ggplot2.

```{r asColorFun}
col_fun <- asColorFun(p, limits = c(-2, 2), na.color = "grey90")

col_fun(c(-2, -1, 0, 1, 2))
col_fun(c(-99, 99, NA))
```

```{r asColorFun-base, fig.height = 3}
image(volcano, col = col_fun(seq(-2, 2, length.out = 64)), axes = FALSE)
```

## `asScaleFillGradient()` and `asScaleColorGradient()`

ggplot2 scales. `show.clip` puts the clip colours on the colourbar,
`clip.width` sets their width, and `...` reaches `scale_*_gradientn()`.

```{r scales, fig.height = 3}
set.seed(1)
grid <- expand.grid(x = seq(0, 1, length.out = 60), y = seq(0, 1, length.out = 60))
grid$z <- with(grid, 2.4 * sin(2.1 * pi * x) * cos(1.6 * pi * y))

ggplot(grid, aes(x, y, fill = z)) +
  geom_raster() +
  asScaleFillGradient(clipped, limits = c(-2, 2)) +
  coord_cartesian(expand = FALSE) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9)
```

```{r color-scale, fig.height = 3}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg, colour = qsec)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  asScaleColorGradient(p, limits = range(mtcars$qsec)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9)
```

## `buildGradient()`

Materialises a specification as a table of stops.

```{r buildGradient}
head(buildGradient(p, limits = c(-2, 2)), 3)
nrow(buildGradient(updateGradient(p, resolution = 20), limits = c(-2, 2)))
```

## `previewGradient()`

Renders a specification as a band, for checking it before committing it to a
figure.

```{r previewGradient}
previewGradient(clipped, limits = c(-2, 2))
```

# Direct builders

These skip the specification object and return a stop table. They take the
curve arguments plus `low.value` and `high.value` in **data units**.

## `sigmoidGradient2()`, `sigmoidGradient3()`, `sigmoidGradientn()`

```{r sigmoid-builders, fig.height = 4.6}
g2 <- sigmoidGradient2("navy", "firebrick", center = 0.7, width = 0.15)
g3 <- sigmoidGradient3("navy", "firebrick", "white", midpoint.value = 0.25)
gn <- sigmoidGradientn(c("black", "navy", "white", "firebrick", "gold"),
                       midpoints = c(0.2, 0.5, 0.75), width = 0.3)

swatch(g2$color, "sigmoidGradient2(center = 0.7, width = 0.15)") /
  swatch(g3$color, "sigmoidGradient3(midpoint.value = 0.25)") /
  swatch(gn$color, "sigmoidGradientn(midpoints = c(0.2, 0.5, 0.75))")
```

`sigmoidGradient3()` takes `midpoint.value` in data units, unlike `midpoints`
elsewhere, because it is a direct builder rather than a specification.

## `linearGradient2()` and `linearGradientn()`

Straight lines instead of logistics, same vocabulary. `width = 1` is an
ordinary ramp; `width < 1` leaves flat regions at both ends.

```{r linear-builders, fig.height = 3.2}
l2 <- linearGradient2("navy", "firebrick")
l2f <- linearGradient2("navy", "firebrick", width = 0.5)

swatch(l2$color, "linearGradient2() -- plain ramp") /
  swatch(l2f$color, "linearGradient2(width = 0.5) -- flat ends")
```

```{r linearGradientn}
head(linearGradientn(c("navy", "white", "firebrick"), midpoints = 0.5), 3)
```

## `customGradientFun()`

Your own mapping, applied once across the whole colour list.

```{r customGradientFun, fig.height = 3.2}
sq <- customGradientFun(c("white", "navy"), mapping_fun = function(x) x^2)
st <- customGradientFun(c("white", "navy"), mapping_fun = function(x) floor(x * 4) / 4)

swatch(sq$color, "mapping_fun = x^2") /
  swatch(st$color, "mapping_fun = floor(x * 4) / 4 -- four bands")
```

A useful case is histogram equalisation, where each quantile of the data gets an
equal share of the colour range:

```{r equalise}
equalise <- function(values, limits) {
  f <- stats::ecdf(values)
  lo <- f(limits[1]); hi <- f(limits[2])
  function(x) {
    y <- f(limits[1] + x * (limits[2] - limits[1]))
    if (hi > lo) (y - lo) / (hi - lo) else y
  }
}

skewed <- rlnorm(4000)
lims <- c(0, unname(quantile(skewed, 0.99)))

eq <- gradientParams(c("white", "navy"), gradient_mode = "custom",
                     mapping_fun = equalise(skewed, lims))

asColorFun(eq, limits = lims)(unname(quantile(skewed, c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9))))
```

# Colour helpers

## `isColor()`

Vectorised; `NA` is always `FALSE`. This validates every colour argument in the
package.

```{r isColor}
isColor(c("red", "#FF0000", "#FF000080", "notacolor", NA))
```

## `colorWheel()`

Hues evenly spaced around the wheel, keeping the base colour's saturation and
value.

```{r colorWheel, fig.height = 1.4}
colorWheel("red", 6)
swatch(colorWheel("red", 12), 'colorWheel("red", 12)')
```

## `colorComplementary()`

The opposite hue. An 8-digit alpha is preserved.

```{r colorComplementary, fig.height = 1.4}
colorComplementary("red")
colorComplementary("#FF000080")

swatch(c("navy", colorComplementary("navy"), "gold", colorComplementary("gold")),
       "pairs: colour and its complement")
```

## `colorSpread()`

`spread - 1` evenly spaced companions, **excluding** the base colour.

```{r colorSpread, fig.height = 1.4}
colorSpread("blue", 4)
swatch(c("blue", colorSpread("blue", 6)), 'blue, then colorSpread("blue", 6)')
```

## `colorBlend()`

One colour part-way from `color2` to `color1`. Defaults to sRGB; it is the only
colour function that drops alpha.

```{r colorBlend, fig.height = 1.4}
colorBlend("red", "blue", 0.5)
colorBlend("black", "white", 0.5)
colorBlend("black", "white", 0.5, space = "Lab")

swatch(vapply(seq(0, 1, 0.1), function(w) colorBlend("red", "blue", w), character(1)),
       "colorBlend(red, blue, weight = 0 .. 1)")
```

## `colorUpdate()`

The same idea on a `shift`/`resolution` scale, defaulting to Lab. `color2` also
accepts `NULL` (towards white), `"complementary"`, or a number, which uses the
`colorSpread()` palette.

```{r colorUpdate, fig.height = 2.6}
colorUpdate("red", "blue", shift = 0)
colorUpdate("red", shift = 20)
colorUpdate("red", "complementary", shift = 30)
colorUpdate("red", 3, shift = 40)

shifts <- function(color2) {
  vapply(seq(0, 100, 10), function(s) colorUpdate("red", color2, shift = s),
         character(1))
}

swatch(shifts("blue"), 'colorUpdate("red", "blue", shift)') /
  swatch(shifts(NULL), 'colorUpdate("red", NULL, shift) -- towards white')
```

## Translucent colours

Gradients interpolate alpha when any input colour is translucent, and omit it
otherwise, so opaque palettes still return 6-digit hex.

```{r alpha}
asColorFun(gradientParams(c("#0000FF00", "#0000FFFF")))(c(0, 0.5, 1))
asColorFun(gradientParams(c("navy", "firebrick")))(c(0, 0.5, 1))
```

# Utilities

## `relativeMidpoint()`

Converts midpoints from data units into the fractions `midpoints` expects --
the most common mistake when wiring brouillet into an existing function.
Vectorised.

```{r relativeMidpoint}
relativeMidpoint(0, c(-2, 2))
relativeMidpoint(c(-1, 1), c(-2, 2))

tryCatch(relativeMidpoint(NA, c(0, 1)), error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
tryCatch(relativeMidpoint(5, c(0, 1)), error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
```

On a limit it warns and nudges inside, which signals that the midpoint cannot be
an interior stop; drop the middle colour and use a two-colour ramp instead.

```{r relativeMidpoint-warn}
withCallingHandlers(
  relativeMidpoint(0, c(0, 1)),
  warning = function(w) {
    message("warned: ", conditionMessage(w))
    invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
  }
)
```

# Running older code

## `gradient_params()`

The one snake_case export. It takes the pre-0.2 arguments -- `sigma1`,
`sigma2`, `inflexpoint1`, `inflexpoint2`, `steepness_preset`, and `midpoints` in
data units -- and returns an ordinary specification that works with every
function above. New code should use `gradientParams()`.

```{r legacy}
old <- gradient_params(colors = c("navy", "white", "firebrick"),
                       midpoints = 50,
                       steepness_preset = "medium")
old

head(buildGradient(old, limits = c(0, 100)), 3)
```

```{r legacy-band}
band(old, limits = c(0, 100), title = 'gradient_params(steepness_preset = "medium")')
```

Legacy specifications interpolate in sRGB, do not rescale the curve, read
`midpoints` as data units, and mirror the lower half of a three-colour gradient
-- all so existing figures regenerate as they looked. They also reproduce two
original quirks deliberately: a non-`NULL` `steepness_preset` overrides explicit
sigmas, and four-or-more-colour gradients build each segment backwards.

```{r legacy-preset}
identical(
  buildGradient(gradient_params(c("red", "blue"), sigma1 = 80, sigma2 = 80))$color,
  buildGradient(gradient_params(c("red", "blue"), steepness_preset = "low"))$color
)
```

Pass `steepness_preset = NULL` to make explicit sigmas take effect.
